book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

chapters.file: ch04 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch05 - Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction frames Rush as a 'thinking man's band': a cult favorite deliberately outside the mainstream whose fusion of virtuosic, structurally complex music with lyrics on social, scientific, and historical themes triggers both fierce devotion and passionate hatred in listeners. It sketches the band's history from its 1968 Toronto cover-band beginnings through Neil Peart's 1974 arrival and the album-oriented-rock success of Moving Pictures ('Tom Sawyer', 'Limelight'), arguing that Rush's lasting achievements come when thoughtful lyrics and progressive/hard music work together. It invites readers to treat each essay as one voice in an ongoing dialogue and to accept that being different, like Rush, is not a bad thing.

chapters.file: ch06 - PART II - The Ebb and Flow of Tidal Fortune.md
ch07 - Houston, We Have a Problem, or, What Goes Up Must Come Down.md
chapters.relation: Auxier interleaves a memoir of sneaking off to Rush's 1977 Memphis concert (the Halloween-weekend ruse with his friend Brice, beers at J-Wags Lounge, the first hangover, and the setlist from 'Bastille Day' through '2112') with a philosophical defense of the band. He rejects the charge that Rush is a vehicle for Ayn Rand's objectivism, arguing Rand was a novelist with 'philosophical moments' whose analogy-built system is not philosophy, and that Peart quickly outgrew her influence by Moving Pictures. Working from Susanne Langer, he claims Rush assimilates lyrics to music (so 'Tom Sawyer' and 'Limelight' need no poetic standard), that music is a 'virtualization' of time creating the illusion of felt life, and that Rush's live processed sounds are second-order virtualizations whose only real test is whether the music is good.

Bowman surveys the fifty-four recorded Rush tributes of 1996-2005, from the Barenaked Ladies quoting the 'Tom Sawyer' swagger riff in 'Grade 9' to DJ Z-Trip's trip-hop remix, Disarray's death-metal version, Deadsy's industrial take, and string-quartet translations, arguing that Rush's ambiguous genre coding is what lets this 'musicians' music' travel across mutually exclusive fan communities. He builds his own 'scholarly meta-remix' interleaving six versions of 'Tom Sawyer' in different keys and meters, and reads the 7/4 instrumental section's fate in each cover. Borrowing Robert Walser's claim that musical meanings are grounded in an ideological field where institutions enforce preferred meanings, he concludes that tribute artists find 'refractive, distorted, and disruptive' meanings in Rush, and that progressive rock served as 'substitute classical music' for working- and lower-middle-class fans.

chapters.file: ch09 - The Heart and Mind United.md
chapters.relation: Sheinbaum argues against the assumption that Rush's rhythmic complexity is 'thinking' music opposed to bodily groove, showing through close listening that 'Subdivisions' (7/8 in 2+2+3 groups), 'Limelight' (4/4 and 3/4 bars interleaved), 'Jacob's Ladder' (alternating 5/4 and 6/4), and the 7/8 passages of 'La Villa Strangiato' all groove while the band retains standard eight-bar phrase structures. He treats meter and hypermeter as Western cultural constructions, and reads Rush's metric deviations as a musical image of the individual resisting a 'conformist social order' (citing Chris McDonald on the individualism Rush shares with Ayn Rand's middle-class virtues). His resolution is dialectical: complex and conventional elements operate as simultaneous poles in synthesis, so mind and body, thought and groove, are united rather than opposed, a point he presses against the racialized mind-body binary in writing about rhythm.

Reuland uses YouTube drum covers of 'The Body Electric', 'Subdivisions', and 'YYZ' to analyze Rush's 'aesthetic of replicability': songs built as artifacts meant to be reproduced note-for-note, signaled by literal codes like the Morse-code intro to 'YYZ' and the binary '1001001' the android of 'The Body Electric' must crack to become human. He explains why critics deride this anti-expressive virtuosity by way of Amiri Baraka's racial coding of technique, Pierre Bourdieu's account of how 'natural' taste is legitimated while studied learning bears class stigma, and Mary Bucholtz's picture of nerds as hyper-white; the fans' literal meritocracy parodies the information economy's promise that skill converts directly into success. Finally he reads 'Limelight' as Rush's skepticism toward performance as a 'gilded cage' of inauthenticity, so that play-along videos recode performance as self-improvement that cannot be faked.

chapters.file: ch11 - He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes.md
chapters.relation: Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.

chapters.file: ch12 - PART II - The Ebb and Flow of Tidal Fortune.md

chapters.relation: Earleywine argues that Rush's lyrics trained a generation in the core moves of cognitive-behavioral therapy, an idea he traces back to Epictetus before Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck rediscovered it against Freudian orthodoxy. He maps specific distortions onto specific songs: 'Witch Hunt' on dichotomous labeling, 'Distant Early Warning' ('black and whites of youth') on all-or-nothing thinking, 'Emotion Detector' on emotional reasoning, 'Vital Signs' and 'Totem' on thoughts altering perception, and 'Subdivisions' ('Conform or be cast out') as realistic critique rather than maladaptive thought. The final step, acting on examined values and savoring the present ('Time Stand Still', 'The Camera Eye', 'Chain Lightning'), makes the songs the incarnation of their own advice: just listen.

Reisch reconstructs the rock-critical case against Rush ('pretentious', 'ridiculous', Greg Kot's jibe that Peart drums 'like he's working out a calculus formula') as resting on an implicit Platonism: the Forms fix what a 'real' rock'n'roll band is, so a band mixing rock with philosophy, literature, and mathematical precision seems to violate the metaphysical grain of the universe rather than merely disappoint a taste. He explains the Forms through Plato's trees and the Form of the song ('La Villa Strangiato' and 'Happy Birthday'), reads Jack Black's 'one atom' praise of Peart as mathematics-as-highest-knowledge, and treats the 'Aristocrats' joke and UFO mocking Geddy Lee as incongruity humor at kinds illicitly combined. Dropping the Platonic metaphysics of kinds collapses the critics' syllogism into a bare insistence that different is bad, which is the revenge Gene Simmons ('What kind of band is Rush? It's Rush.') and Billy Corgan ('they just don't fit in a neat box') already delivered.

chapters.file: ch15 - Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song.md
chapters.relation: Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.

Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.

Kreuger applies Derrida's 'Differance' to how Rush gets valued: Hugh Syme's starman, pentagram, and bunnies are signs whose meaning defers down a chain, so no description of Geddy Lee ever touches the thing itself, and the band's twenty-four gold albums (economic value) never settle the contested question of cultural value that critics deny and fans affirm. Time defers value too: 'Time Stand Still' and the concert ticket sell a moment already gone, bootlegs and leaks chase the unrepeatable experience, and radio distance once hid songs like '2112' from value. 'The Spirit of Radio' carries the thesis in its own lyric, 'bearing a gift beyond price, almost free', where 'the words of the profits' on the studio walls measure sold value against integrity, and deferral finally emerges as Derrida's 'condition of possibility' that lets Rush's cultural value recover through Colbert, Rock Band, and I Love You, Man.

chapters.file: ch18 - Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love.md
chapters.relation: Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: American philosopher of mind and aesthetics (Feeling and Form) who holds that each art creates a 'semblance' of felt experience in a virtual space or time, and that mixed art forms obey a 'principle of assimilation'.
holes.why: Chapter 7 builds its entire account of Rush on Langer: lyrics are assimilated to music, music is 'virtualized time' creating the illusion of felt life, and processed live sounds are second-order virtualizations.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism, a creed of rational self-interest and individualism conveyed through fiction such as The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged.
holes.why: Chapter 7 argues Peart's early lyrics ('Anthem', '2112') borrowed Rand's objectivism before he outgrew it, and dissects why Rand counts as a novelist with philosophical moments rather than a philosopher.

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher of Distinction who argued that taste is class-coded: 'natural' early immersion in culture confers legitimacy and ease, while belated, studied learning bears a visible stigma.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses Bourdieu's distinction between natural and studied cultural learning to explain why critics stigmatize Rush's autodidact, note-perfect fans and why the band's studied virtuosity reads as class-marked.

holes.name: Pure Language and the Task of the Translator
holes.what: Benjamin's view (in 'The Task of the Translator', not the aura essay) that translation is an echo called into the 'language forest' whose inevitable variations and errors release a 'pure language' beyond original and copy.
holes.why: Chapter 11 leans on this essay to defend imperfect Rush covers, live variations, and outright errors ('Turn the Page', the Feedback album) as completions of the work rather than corruptions of a Platonic original.
